rationale: A wins because it keeps the launch honest and sells only the stories the facts can carry: "The SVB collapse itself is not a current peg and must not be dressed as one" is exactly the guardrail a founder needs. B has usable bones, but it opens with "Two Years After SVB" even though the timestamp is June 9, 2026 and SVB failed in March 2023; that is not nuance, that is a calendar error. A makes proof operational; B too often turns hypotheses into headlines, especially "Mercury Has 200,000 Business Customers. It Just Started Pitching Them Personally."
gaps_in_A: "What the SVB windfall became" overclaims the supplied facts. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB; it does not prove a windfall in deposits, customers, or revenue.
"the bank startups fled to" and "business-only bank" blur the charter issue A correctly flags elsewhere. Call Mercury a fintech or banking platform when the no-charter angle is in play.

"the obvious wedge is the founders and employees" is a smart hypothesis, but still a hypothesis. The set handles this in proof, but the angle copy should stay more conditional until waitlist priority is confirmed.
gaps_in_B: "Two Years After SVB" is factually wrong against the supplied timestamp. June 9, 2026 is more than three years after the March 2023 SVB collapse.

"Mercury's name recognition was built entirely" and "stepped up when SVB failed" are unsupported embellishments. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that SVB built the whole brand or that Mercury played savior.
"runs opposite to the consumer-to-business neobank trajectory most competitors have tried" invents market context not supplied in the update. That needs evidence, not confidence.
"It Just Started Pitching Them Personally" asserts a cross-sell motion the facts do not establish. Invite-only with a waitlist does not mean Mercury is pitching existing business customers.
